structure.title: Chapters 1–3 · The door and the will
structure.text: A Sunday walk brings a neglected door to Utterson's attention. His cousin tells him about a child trampled in the street and a cheque signed by a respectable man. The lawyer already has a document in his safe that makes the story sound dangerously plausible.

structure.title: Chapters 4–8 · Visitors outside the house
structure.text: As the violence grows more public, the friends protecting Jekyll find themselves asking servants about his visitors and studying his handwriting. Their good manners have always allowed a gentleman considerable privacy. Now that habit makes it hard to decide when to break down a door.

structure.title: Chapters 9–10 · Two documents opened late
structure.text: An account by Lanyon and a statement by Jekyll supply the voices that Utterson's discretion kept out of reach. Both men have reasons for the order and language in which they give their evidence. Knowing what happened still leaves the question of who takes responsibility for it.

people.name: Utterson
people.text: He takes pride in standing by people who have got themselves into trouble. The virtue suits a solicitor entrusted with confidential business. It also gives a man who is harming others an unusually patient friend.

people.name: Jekyll and Lanyon
people.text: The two share a social world and disagree about the limits of legitimate experiment. Their professional quarrel makes it possible to discount a friend's alarm as the predictable prejudice of a colleague.

context.title: A respectable name is negotiable property
context.text: Cheques, wills and letters transfer wealth or authority because somebody recognises the signature. Utterson tries to follow the connection between Hyde and Jekyll through this paperwork. Each document can prove an association without explaining what either man wanted.

notice.text: Hear the failures to describe Hyde.
notice.why: Witnesses agree that he inspires revulsion. Asked for a particular deformity they could point to in court, they falter. Stevenson lets a unanimous impression acquire the force of evidence while keeping its precise object elusive.

notice.text: Map the entrances before deciding which rooms belong together.
notice.why: A fine front door receives dinner guests. An ugly doorway opens off another street. Utterson's walk round the block gives architecture a role in how long a social distinction can survive.

opening: A respectable doctor changes his will to leave everything to a man his friends find repulsive. Nobody can explain the connection, and the doctor refuses to discuss it. His lawyer suspects blackmail and begins asking questions, hoping to rescue a friend’s reputation before something worse happens. Stevenson follows that investigation through locked doors, evasive answers, and a London where respectability offers very little assurance about what a person might be capable of when nobody is watching.
